articles.title: Living with tinnitus can be distressing. So what can you do about it?
articles.summary: Tinnitus affects millions of people and it can take many different forms. But there are therapies that can help make it more bearable. For some it’s a high-pitched mosquito whine; for others it’s a low bass hum.
body: Whatever form it takes, tinnitus – hearing sounds like ringing, buzzing or hissing when no external noise is there – can be extremely distressing because it’s quite literally in your head; there is no escaping it. Given that at least one-quarter of the population report experiencing tinnitus at some stage in their life, it’s surprising how little is understood about why.

“The theory that’s most supported at the moment is that there’s some sort of change in the hearing pathway, and the nerves in the hearing pathway are basically firing more than they should do,” says Dr Emma Laird, an audiologist at La Trobe University in Melbourne. “We’re hearing this increased activity as that tinnitus sound.”

There is no cure for tinnitus but the good news is that there is a variety of treatment approaches – audiological, psychological, physiotherapeutic and technological – that can be effective at helping people to manage the condition. “I’ve had tinnitus for probably 20 years now,” Laird says. “Because I’ve habituated to it – so my brain can just pop it at the back of my head – it’s not causing distress day to day.”
points: Tinnitus affects millions of people and it can take many different forms.
But there are therapies that can help make it more bearable.
For some it’s a high-pitched mosquito whine; for others it’s a low bass hum.

articles.title: Horl 3 review: an easy (and fun!) way to keep your knives sharp and at the ready
articles.summary: This sharpener is easy to use and does the job well enough to please a professional chef. The seven best air fryers, tried and tested in a food lab. Sign up for the Filter US newsletter, your weekly guide to buying fewer, better things.
body: I n every cooking class that I teach, knife sharpening is the first lesson my students learn. Dull knives are inefficient and dangerous – a dull blade can slide right off the curvature of an onion into the flesh of the hand holding it.

At the Drexel Food Lab, where I’m a certified research chef and culinary educator, we use a Tormek T2 Pro Kitchen Knife Sharpener, donated by the company, to sharpen our knives. It is a dream piece of equipment that can sharpen any knife we throw at it, from a pile of our classes’ cheap stainless steel Dexter kitchen knives to a high-end carbon steel Japanese slicer for our instructors’ use.

But at nearly $900 and 14lbs, the T2 is overkill if you’re not running a professional kitchen. It’s driving a Lamborghini in stop-and-go city traffic. For easy home use, I recommend the Horl 3, a simple-to-learn rolling knife sharpener with a stand that holds the knife in place at the optimal angle. Co-founder Otmar Horl, an engineer, together with his son, Timo, a graphic designer and barbecue enthusiast, designed the first rolling knife sharpening system that became the Horl 3 in the basement of their family home, where they produced the first 200 units by hand.
points: This sharpener is easy to use and does the job well enough to please a professional chef.

articles.title: ‘She changed the beauty industry’: how Charlotte Mensah brought black hair into the spotlight
articles.summary: A new exhibition in London celebrates the influential hairstylist whose clients include Janelle Monáe and Zadie Smith. She explains her story – and why she’s on a mission to ensure stylists are trained to work with all hair types.
body: When Charlotte Mensah was a young child growing up in Accra, Ghana in the 1970s, she would spend hours watching her aunties having their hair intricately threaded, an ancient African technique where hair is wrapped tightly using yarn or thread. She didn’t know then that she would go on to become one of the most influential hairdressers in the UK. Renowned for championing natural black hair textures, she has worked as hairstylist to singers Janelle Monáe and Erykah Badu, and the writer Zadie Smith.
According to Smith, in an essay she penned about Mensah’s magic earlier this year: “Charlotte can make a great mane of braids appear where previously there were only split ends and hair loss.”

A three-time winner of afro hairdresser of the year and the first black woman to be inducted into the British Hairdressing Awards Hall of Fame in 2018: the extraordinary course of her 40-year-long career is now the subject of an exhibition, Charlotte Mensah: Community Matters in west London. It charts her rise from growing up in the Ghanaian capital, through her early days as a junior hairdresser in London’s West End in the 80s, to styling celebrities for magazine covers.
points: A new exhibition in London celebrates the influential hairstylist whose clients include Janelle Monáe and Zadie Smith.

articles.title: CondéFuture Program 2025/26: a Year in Review
articles.summary: CondéFuture, led by Condé Nast’s creative and editorial teams, is a global initiative that aims to inspire and nurture future generations of multimedia creative talent.
body: "It was really stressful," Sydney said. "I waited until after APs, and journalism isn't my strong suit." As her deadline closed in, she got help from the copy editing team, who polished her articles in the final stretch. One of them told her she could Slack any time she needed something. By June, she'd written the magazine's cover story herself, along with two additional features.

Sydney is part of the latest cohort of CondéFuture, Condé Nast's two-year media enrichment program in partnership with Educational Alliance for New York City high school students. Students entered the program as juniors, spending Wednesday evenings through the academic year inside Condé Nast offices while balancing classes, sports, and other extracurriculars.

CondéFuture is a program designed to expose NYC youth from marginalized communities to a media industry that has historically under or misrepresented the ethnic and socioeconomic backgrounds they represent. Through mentorship and project based learning led by Condé Nast's creative teams, these young people learn from experts and bring their unique perspective into the work.

articles.title: Kate Middleton Knows A Winning Outfit Formula When She Sees One
articles.summary: For everything from Prince George’s school drop-off to hospital visits, this stunning color has become a fashion favorite for the Princess of Wales.
body: In June, the Princess of Wales became the first royal to complete the National Three Peaks Challenge. One of the UK’s most grueling hikes, it involves climbing the highest mountains in Scotland (Ben Nevis), England (Scafell Pike) and Wales (Snowdon) within 24 hours. No mean feat, of course, but Catherine nobly rose to the challenge to raise money for The Royal Marsden Cancer Charity, which works to improve access to holistic cancer care, having supported the Princess through her own diagnosis in 2024.

Now 20 months in remission, today Catherine returned to the Royal Marsden for a surprise visit, speaking to staff and patients and observing how the funds raised through her Three Peaks Challenge are being put to use. For the occasion, she wore an emerald dress by eco-conscious label Suzannah London, which she previously wore to the Anna Freud Centre during Mental Health Awareness Week in 2023. So fond is she of the style that she owns it in multiple color ways—though this particular shade of green is fast becoming a favorite.
The Princess with chief nurse, Mairead Griffith and chief medical officer, Sanjay Popat.

articles.title: Checking In! Valentino Vendetta Took Over an Iconic LA Motel with Dakota Johnson, Alexander Skarsgård, and Solange Knowles
articles.summary: Valentino Beauty celebrated the launch of its Vendetta fragrances alongside Dakota Johnson, Alexander Skarsgård, Keke Palmer, Solange Knowles, Brooklyn Beckham, Nicola Peltz Beckham, Sophia Bush, and soccer star Ashlyn Harris.
body: The setting was a natural continuation of the Vendetta campaign starring Johnson and Skarsgård, who recently spoke to Vogue about their first project together. Shot by Inez & Vinoodh, the ad follows the pair through a relationship that Johnson described as “quite intense and fiery.” There’s fast cars, a countryside setting, and, according to Skarsgård, some rather terrifying driving on Johnson’s part.

At the Safari Inn, no detail went untouched. Retro automobiles lined the motel, some with their trunks filled to the brim with bottles of Vendetta, while additional fragrances waited outside the doors of motel rooms. An old-school telephone booth doubled as a photo moment, extending the campaign’s lovers-on-the-run aesthetic across the grounds.

The scents offer two interpretations of the Vendetta story. Vendetta Donna centers on tuberose, red orange, and sandalwood—a result that Johnson called “intoxicating, but still soft.” Vendetta Uomo, meanwhile, features ginger, cinnamon liqueur, and patchouli; a full-circle moment for its face, Skarsgård, who revealed that he wore the original Valentino Vendetta to his school dances more than three decades ago.

articles.title: “New York Is My Paris”: Conner Ives on Showing Across the Pond Ahead of His New York Fashion Week Debut
articles.summary: For London-based Conner Ives, his New York Fashion Week debut represents all he has been working towards. Of course, this includes some gilded glamour and cheeky T-shirts, too.
body: For London-based designer Conner Ives, New York Fashion Week has always been more than a homecoming; it’s a North Star. “The thought of doing a show in New York has always been there, and people would kind of make fun of me because I saw New York as my Paris,” Ives tells Vogue ahead of his stateside debut. But does this location change-up classify him as a British designer? In the most technical sense of the term, Ives would argue maybe. Ives was born and raised in Westchester County, New York, where he first developed his love for art and costume design; however, it wasn’t until he moved across the pond in 2014 to attend Central Saint Martins in London that his career really began.

Always one for archetypes, this season’s bridal look tips its hat to a lesser-known New York film, Jonathan Glazer’s Birth, starring Nicole Kidman. “I think that is just such a perfect piece of cinematic New York,” he explains. “The original husband dies in Central Park in the opening scene as it’s snowing, Lauren Bacall plays her mother on the Upper East Side—it’s like you couldn't write a more New York story, and I think that, to me, was really the kind of crown jewel of what we’re doing here.”
